tldr: Researchers have developed "RAEM," a novel framework that enables quadruped robots to autonomously explore and map multi-floor buildings with stairs. By smartly combining a local tomography map, a local 3D grid map, and an elevation-aware global topological graph, RAEM limits computational overhead, prevents falls on stairs, and avoids path disconnections—achieving continuous autonomous exploration across a 5-floor stairwell on a real robot.
hero_caption: Overall concept of RAEM. Four key components work together to achieve robust multi-floor exploration: (a) an elevation-aware global topological graph that captures overlapping multi-floor structures, (b) staircase center alignment of viewpoints to prevent wobbling while climbing, (c) local grid search recovery when missing point clouds cause topological disconnections, and (d) automatic pruning of physically unreachable viewpoints.
overview:
Quadruped robots offer superior traversability compared to wheeled platforms for exploring complex indoor environments like buildings and industrial plants. However, most existing ground-robot exploration algorithms rely on 2D grids or elevation maps, making it impossible to handle overlapping floor structures and staircases. While tomography-based representations capture multi-layer traversability by slicing 3D space, continuously updating a global tomography map online incurs prohibitive computational costs, causing real-time exploration planning to break down. Moreover, when looking up staircases, the shallow angle of LiDAR beams produces sparse and fragmented point clouds, resulting in scattered viewpoints and path disconnections that can cause the robot to tip over while turning.

To tackle these challenges, the authors proposed "RAEM," a hierarchical framework that decouples local 3D geometric analysis from global topological representation. Lightweight local tomography maps and local 3D grid maps are generated strictly around the robot using GPU parallelization, while a sparse, elevation-aware topological graph is incrementally built on the CPU for global routing. In addition, RAEM introduces a staircase center alignment strategy that places viewpoints along the center of stair treads to curb abrupt yaw variations, as well as a dual path searching mechanism that finds alternative paths on the local grid whenever the global topology is disconnected.

In evaluations across four multi-floor environments in the Gazebo simulator—featuring spiral and switchback staircases—RAEM was compared with leading baselines (TARE, FAEL, and HPHS). While none of the baselines could advance past the first floor, RAEM consistently achieved a 100% exploration completion rate across all scenes. Furthermore, deployed on a real Unitree Go2 quadruped using only its onboard Jetson Orin NX, RAEM successfully performed continuous autonomous exploration of a 5-floor stairwell, proving its high reliability and computational stability in real-world environments.
contributions: Proposed a hybrid traversability representation combining a GPU-accelerated local tomography/3D grid map and a global topological graph, completely avoiding the computational burden of updating a global tomography map.

Constructed an ultra-fast GPU pipeline that explicitly classifies local 3D grid cells into traversable, free, and occupied spaces based on the vertical geometric relationships between local tomography slices.
Introduced a staircase center alignment strategy to prevent scattered viewpoints caused by sparse stair point clouds, eliminating the risk of quadruped roll-overs from abrupt yaw turns.
Established a dual path searching mechanism that autonomously recovers safe ascent paths directly from the local grid when the global topology becomes disconnected.

sections.heading: Why is multi-floor exploration so difficult for quadruped robots?
sections.summary: Autonomous multi-floor exploration by ground robots faces fundamental limitations when using traditional planar map representations, which fail to handle vertically overlapping structures and stairs. Applying navigation-oriented tomography maps directly to exploration introduces massive computational overhead, and sparse point cloud returns on stairs can destabilize the robot. RAEM solves these issues by decoupling local and global spatial representations and employing stair-specific planning strategies.
sections.details:
For 3D surveying and facility inspection, ground robots offer higher payload capacities and longer operational endurance than aerial drones. However, most conventional ground exploration methods rely on 2D occupancy grids or 2.5D elevation maps (which represent terrain with a single height value per cell). These methods crush multi-floor buildings into a single plane, completely failing in environments with overlapping ceilings, floors, and staircases.

While tomography maps designed for multi-floor navigation can represent traversability across layered structures, directly applying them to online autonomous exploration runs into two major roadblocks:
- First, maintaining a global tomography map and frequently replanning paths on it creates a massive computational bottleneck, undermining the real-time demands of chasing newly discovered frontiers.
- Second, because onboard LiDARs are mounted low, the shallow incidence angle when looking up staircases leaves point clouds sparse and fragmented. As a result, generated viewpoints scatter in a zigzag pattern, prompting the quadruped to make aggressive yaw turns on steps that risk fatal tip-overs, or causing connectivity drops that break path planning entirely.

RAEM (Robust Autonomous Exploration for Multi-Floor Environments) breaks through these bottlenecks by cleanly separating local geometric analysis from global topology. By restricting GPU-accelerated local tomography and 3D grid mapping to a bounded volume around the robot and incrementally expanding an elevation-aware topological graph for the rest of the world, RAEM drastically cuts computation times while enabling stable, robust multi-floor exploration.

captions.F1: The four core features of RAEM: (a) constructing an elevation-aware topological graph to represent multi-floor overlap, (b) aligning viewpoints with the center of stair treads to ensure straight-line climbing, (c) dual path searching that switches to local grid search during topological disconnections, and (d) pruning unreachable viewpoints once points accumulate during ascent.

sections.heading: The technological gap between drones, planar rovers, and multi-floor navigation
sections.summary: Drone exploration frameworks capture 3D free space well, but lack the terrain traversability analysis essential for legged robots. Conversely, existing ground-robot exploration methods are constrained by planar assumptions, while multi-floor navigation maps incur search overheads too heavy for real-time online exploration.
sections.details:
Prior work related to multi-floor exploration broadly falls into three categories:

- UAV (Drone) Exploration:
Because drones can freely fly through 3D space, approaches like FUEL and ECHO typically employ 3D occupancy grids (such as UFOMap or OctoMap) to extract frontiers on the boundaries of free space and build topological graphs through open air. However, these methods only evaluate whether a volume is unobstructed; they completely ignore whether the ground slope or step heights are traversable for legged robots.

- AGV (Ground Robot) Exploration:
Prominent systems like TARE and FAEL use 2D grids or elevation maps for computational efficiency. While exceptionally effective on a single floor, they squash height into a single 2D layer, rendering them incapable of recognizing stairs or multiple stacked floors and structurally unable to explore entire buildings.

- Multi-Floor Navigation:
Approaches like PCT-Planner introduced global tomography maps composed of multiple 2.5D slices to model overhangs and multi-layer traversable areas. However, these were designed for navigation on pre-built, complete maps. Re-evaluating such global representations online amidst sparse, continuous point cloud streams causes computational complexity to explode. They also lack robustness against low-angle observation failures under stairwells.

RAEM bridges this divide, delivering an exploration representation that models multi-floor 3D structures efficiently while remaining resilient to physical instability on challenging footings.

sections.heading: A hybrid local-global architecture with dedicated stair safety mechanisms
sections.summary: RAEM generates a local tomography map and an explicitly categorized lightweight 3D grid at high speed on the GPU, while incrementally updating an elevation-aware topological graph on the CPU. On staircases, a tread-centering viewpoint alignment and a dual path searching mechanism ensure safe, continuous climbing even when global connectivity drops.
sections.details:
The complete architecture operates as a heterogeneous pipeline dividing responsibilities between the GPU and CPU:

- System Overview (IV-A):
Highly parallel local operations—such as point-cloud geometric analysis and grid construction—are offloaded to the GPU. Meanwhile, managing the global topological graph, frontier extraction, and global path planning are handled by the CPU.

- Local Tomography Map Construction (IV-C):
Within a fixed-size local bounding box $\mathcal{B}_{local}$ centered on the robot, point clouds are sliced using equidistant horizontal planes. Each slice $S_k$ records floor elevation, ceiling elevation, and traversal cost. The system checks whether the clearance between floor and ceiling meets minimum requirements and verifies that the floor slope is safe, assigning high traversal costs to dangerous cliff edges.

- GPU-based Local 3D Grid Generation (IV-D):
From the 2.5D slice data of the tomography map, GPU threads instantly classify vertical columns into four states: unknown, occupied, free, and traversable. Only the single cell immediately above the floor is marked traversable, while spaces bounded by a lower slice's ceiling and an upper slice's floor are treated as architectural slabs and marked occupied. Traversable cells are then horizontally dilated by one cell to reinforce connectivity on stairs.

- Slice-wise Obstacle Extraction and Global Topology Construction (IV-E, IV-F):
Untraversable cells in each slice are projected onto a 2D plane to build 2D kd-trees, enabling ultra-fast obstacle distance queries. Using these distance checks alongside collision testing against the local grid, vertices are sampled and connected across traversable areas, incrementally expanding an elevation-aware global topological graph that captures multi-floor structures.

- Viewpoint Generation and Staircase Center Alignment (IV-G):
Candidate viewpoints are generated after clustering frontiers to reduce planning overhead. When staircases are detected, traversable cells are grouped via region growing, and viewpoints are strictly projected onto the geometric centerline of the stair treads to prevent missteps.

- Dual Path Searching (IV-H):
If point clouds under a staircase are too sparse to sustain topological edges, a fallback mechanism performs A-star pathfinding directly over traversable cells in the local 3D grid. This guarantees a safe guidance path to the floor above even before global topology is restored.

sections.heading: Flawless simulation runs and autonomous conquest of a 5-floor stairwell
sections.summary: In four multi-floor simulation scenes in Gazebo, RAEM was the only method among four evaluated to achieve a 100% exploration rate. Ablations confirmed an 18x speedup via GPU mapping and proved that stair-centering prevents fatal rollovers. On a real Unitree Go2 robot, RAEM conquered a 5-floor stairwell running entirely on onboard compute.
sections.details:
The framework was validated extensively in both simulation and real-world experiments:

- Simulation Comparisons (V-A):
Four challenging multi-floor environments were created: a 3-floor building with spiral stairs ($scene\_1$), a 3-floor building with switchback stairs ($scene\_2$), a multi-room 2-floor layout ($scene\_3$), and a 4-floor environment with narrow corridors and blind corners ($scene\_4$). Compared against TARE, FAEL, and HPHS, TARE and FAEL failed to climb beyond the first floor due to their planar assumptions, while the local-planner-reliant HPHS suffered frequent breakdowns in complex areas. RAEM achieved a perfect 100% completion rate across all 20 runs per scene.

- Computational Cost and Ablations (V-B to V-F):
The average computation time per planning iteration was under 0.1 seconds in corridor scenes and around 0.2 seconds in open spaces. Generating the local 3D grid on the GPU was roughly 18 times faster than on the CPU. Switching viewpoint generation from dense sampling (FAEL style) to frontier clustering cut compute times roughly in half, maintaining responsive planning regardless of space size.

- Validating Stair-Specific Modules (V-E, V-F):
When staircase center alignment was disabled, aggressive yaw turns occurred on steps, resulting in a fatal roll-over and tumble in 1 out of 20 runs. Enabling center alignment achieved 20 out of 20 stable, straight climbs. Comparing dual path searching against topology-only routing improved the exploration success rate from 12/20 to 20/20, demonstrating its robustness against degraded observations.

- Real-World Experiments (V-G):
Deployed on a Unitree Go2 equipped with a Mid-360S LiDAR, Fast-LIO2 odometry, and an onboard Jetson Orin NX (16GB), RAEM was tested in real buildings. In a 5-floor stairwell ($stairwell$), the robot autonomously climbed across four landings and continuous flights of stairs to reach the top floor. It also executed continuous exploration without pausing across two different 2-floor building layouts and a large entrance hall ($lobby$).

sections.heading: Summary and outlook: Scaling toward multi-robot cooperative exploration
sections.summary: RAEM successfully establishes the first practical, robust online autonomous exploration framework for quadruped robots in multi-floor environments by uniting local geometric mapping with global elevation-aware topology. Dedicated algorithms resolve sensory and dynamic instabilities on stairs, setting the stage for future extensions to multi-robot teams.
sections.details:
This work introduces RAEM, an autonomous exploration framework tailored to both the locomotion dynamics of quadruped robots and the geometric complexity of multi-floor architecture.

Addressing the computational bottleneck of global tomography maps, RAEM decouples local analysis (tomography and 3D grids) from global planning (topological graphs), achieving real-time responsiveness without sacrificing 3D awareness. Furthermore, it tackles two practical hazards in robotic stair climbing—rollovers from erratic viewpoints and path drops from sparse point clouds—via staircase center alignment and dual path searching.

The authors plan to release their full source code to the community upon paper acceptance. Future work will extend this framework toward multi-robot collaborative exploration, enabling fleets of quadrupeds to coordinate and map expansive high-rises and complex facilities in parallel.

takeaways: Decoupling spatial representations into fine-grained local geometric analysis (GPU) and lightweight global topology (CPU) is an effective architectural pattern for resource-constrained exploration.
In hazardous terrains like stairs, planners must actively enforce dynamic stability—such as geometric tread alignment to prevent yaw swings—alongside informational utility.

Leveraging the fact that sensor coverage improves as the robot advances, using local grid search as a fallback for temporary topological cuts is a broadly applicable strategy for ground robots with constrained sensor fields of view.
limitations: The current system is designed specifically for ascending stair exploration and does not explicitly support descending stairs to move between floors.
Stair descent is currently unsupported due to blind spots from the LiDAR's fixed 45-degree downward pitch and the control/dynamic stability challenges of descending steps on a quadruped.

Because Fast-LIO2 is used for state estimation, odometry drift remains a risk in long, featureless corridors; during experiments, temporary obstacles were manually placed in some areas to prevent the robot from entering such corridors.
